_doc: Day-by-day narrative + companions for the Japan trip. Day 1 = 2026-04-18 (land day). Day 10 = 2026-04-27 (return). Team members are pseudonymized for privacy.

trip.title: Japan — April 2026
trip.tagline: A long way to get there, and worth every step.
trip.intro: Bryan was nervous. Everyone he'd talked to about Japan called it their biggest culture shock with any new country. He couldn't agree more. The Caribbean is a cruise. Europe is confusing but navigable. Japan was an alien world — and that was the point. The trip was a work trip with personal exploration on both ends. First time in Japan. The hardest culture shock of his life. And the most rewarding.
trip.team: Six people, six passports. Five internal experts from five different countries — Bryan's manager, the director of product, the Japan customer success manager, the chief researcher, and Bryan — plus the manager's wife, a sixth nationality. Bryan originally took the Japan account for no commission, just to learn it and write it on a resume. The business exploded; he barely slid into the trip and is so glad he did. Young, niche, hungry. Top of the game at very specific things.
trip.stakes: Small company, few resources. Everyone knew if the trip didn't produce, there wouldn't be another one like it. A handful of existing customers, a handful of partners, a handful of key prospects — enough to work with. Bryan was the energy guy. He took that seriously.
trip.discipline: Almost clean of everything for the trip. Caffeine and nicotine. No prescriptions, not even allergy meds. Zyns and multivitamins were the only risks taken in a country with very strict laws. Needed to be sharp intellectually, emotionally, physically, spiritually — all at once, which is almost impossible. Something usually gives. He gave it a real go.
trip.routine: 5 AM wake-up. Meditation, 10 minutes — letting thoughts come and go. Then plan the day: how am I feeling, what do I need to do, what do I want to do. Walk to the only thing open — 7-Eleven, Lawson, or Family Mart. Rice triangles (rice and beans, or rice and tuna, $1-2). Coffee chat with whoever was behind the counter if no one was in line. Wander the city at dawn when it was almost his. Gym opens at 6 (he tried to start at 5:30 the first day and got politely redirected by the front desk). Mostly upper body and stretching — stretch the Shinto out, no dumb middle-aged injury. Public bath after, once or twice a day. L-shaped hot tub, fully nude, shower first, no chlorine, water hot as hell. Felt like heaven after a day of walking. Hotel breakfast at 7, usually first in. After Day 2, switched from Japanese to greek-yogurt + fruit + eggs + bread — every other meal would be fish and meat, fiber needed to come from somewhere.
trip.wandering: Get lost on purpose. Wander best with an interesting target — weave and turn to get there. The most ADHD exploring: see something in the distance, walk that way, two-hour detour, eventually back on course.
trip.standing_out: Couldn't blend in. Towered over everyone. Few Americans on the streets, none as tall. Stares were rare and mostly came from little kids — wanted to make faces, never did. Quiet, respectful, leave a small trace. Asked locals to correct his pronunciation when they were up for it. Got offered silverware once and was briefly offended before realizing only tourist spots even kept silverware out.
trip.this_is_the_way: Everything in Japan was efficient by design. Lines marked. No confusion. Got pointed back to a line marker by an older Japanese woman once — was six inches off. Respectfully moved six inches left. Saw maybe four people jaywalk all trip. Felt Apple-like — minimalist by intent, not by lack. Rules exist for a reason; the reason is things go the way they're supposed to.
trip.food: Surprisingly little seasoning. Bryan thought maybe it was the quality — high-quality meat doesn't need to be hidden. Probably also the minimalist design ethos: cook it perfectly, let it stand. Salt and a few spices, that was it. Raw egg as a dipping sauce — hot meat dunked in just-warm raw egg — was a revelation. Said no to chicken hearts (other organs and cartilage already done; stomach asked for a break). Matcha everywhere. Tea everywhere. Coffee kept him moving.
trip.team_rhythm: Met around 9 most mornings, after his routine. Doug sometimes came straight from bed, working on his laptop. High-profile meetings meant nerves, translations, edits and re-edits. New solution pitch being built mid-trip. Out till 9 or 10 most nights. A couple of late ones. Called Kel most nights when he got back. Clair was the team's walking yelp — Google-Map-pinned restaurants planned weeks ahead, perfect for a Director of Product doubling as restaurant chauffeur. They waited in a lot of organized lines. He hated standing and waiting. The food was always worth it.

days.title: Land + Ginza first night
days.opening_quote: A long way to get there, and worth every step.
days.summary: Lands at HND 15:55, fourteen and a half hours of flying still in the bones. Passport panic at immigration — turned out to be buried deep in a pocket, not lost. A two-machine immigration ritual no foreigner seemed to crack on the first try. The train station gets worse: dozes off mid-rush-hour, looks up at Google Maps and is twenty minutes south of where he should be. Reverses course, gives up on trains, books a hotel. Planes, trains, and literally automobiles. A thirty-minute airport trip turned into three hours — the foretelling for the whole trip: a long way to get there, worth every step. Shower, hits the streets. Tokyo lands like an alien world: NYC vibes with shrines tucked between high-rises, tiny restaurants lining the alleys. First meal: sits down and cautiously watches other people eat before starting. Discovers Kabuki-za next door at 22:16.

days.title: Tsukiji to Senso-ji to Park
days.summary: A 15-hour cross-Tokyo Sunday. Met up with crew that morning — they had their own plans, gave city tips, sent him wandering. Pre-dawn Tsukiji, past the great domed Hongan-ji. Then Nakamise-dori climbing toward Senso-ji, vendor-lined and jammed. First shrine ritual: 100 yen (about 68 cents), one bow, two claps, prayer, one more bow. Eavesdropped on every tour guide that passed. Drew his first omikuji from the cylinder of numbered wooden rods — #31. Pulled the slip. THE LEAST FORTUNATE. Lowest of the low. After the initial flash of 'burn it,' decided to keep it — the most ridiculous, on-the-nose first-fortune in Japan, treasured. Then Meiji Jingu's camphor tree and ema wall, where he drew a second omikuji 'from the empress' — better luck, but the first stays his favorite. ADHD wandering filled the gaps: see something in the distance, walk that way, two-hour detour, then back on course. Capped with a drugstore haul.

days.title: Team arrives + Tonkatsu
days.opening_quote: Six people. Six passports. Five different countries plus a plus-one.
days.summary: The team lands. Five internal experts, five different passports — manager, director of product, customer success lead, chief researcher, Bryan — plus the manager's wife, a sixth nationality. Bryan took the Japan account originally for no commission, just to learn it and write it on a resume; the business exploded and earned him the last seat on the trip. Monday: a prep day with no external meetings — alignment, energy, getting in the same room. A dawn konbini coffee, a hipster breakfast bowl, and the morning Bryan picked up his goshuin book — the stamp book he'd carry to every shrine. Tonkatsu group lunch, an afternoon city walk, a drugstore run with a coworker, and a basement robatayaki team dinner — staff in traditional dress, open grills, the heave-ho chant across the bar.

days.title: First MoD + teamLab + yakitori
days.opening_quote: Yes — how many, and how soon can we start?
days.summary: The team's first real performance. After the 5 AM gym-and-bath routine and a coworking-space morning, a quick tsukemen lunch at Tsujita in Ginza, then the first MoD meeting in Ichigaya — a brand-new prospect, the whole team spread across the room reading each other's hand signals. Trees grew up the stairwells of the government building; even here, everything had a spirit. When the prospect asked to try some licenses, Bryan put up a hand to quiet the team and said the only thing you say: 'Yes — how many, and how soon can we start?' Walking out hyped, he shoved his boss with excitement; his boss did not love it. The team-building was teamLab Borderless — the water-floor room, the overwhelming sunflower room where he thought of Kel and missed her, the wave room he sat in a while 'to get washed,' the icicle Crystal Universe. Dinner was yakitori, Clair's pick, all weird things — Bryan managed one chicken heart, decided that was enough, and quietly switched to ramen.

days.title: NSSOL day + Kaiseki
days.opening_quote: I felt so humbled. I never thought I would conduct business in a Tokyo highrise.
days.summary: Bryan suits up for an NSSOL deep-dive in a Tokyo highrise — twice that day he photographed the city falling away below the window — and ends with a kaiseki dinner at Akasaka Saryo: a private tatami room, a gold-leaf cherry-blossom folding screen, an individual donabe pot at every setting, the full spring course menu. Alex and the NSSOL host researcher clowned a back-to-back photo by the restaurant's zen rock garden.

days.title: Zojoji + Ministry of Defense + Suimei
days.summary: Morning at the Imperial Palace outer moat and East Gardens gate, then Zojoji beneath Tokyo Tower — where Bryan unknowingly walked the Kumano Jinja, a crow shrine: its messenger is the Yatagarasu, the three-legged crow that guided a lost emperor through the mountains. Quietly heavy too: the Sentai Kosodate Jizo, rows of small statues for unborn children. A team gyudon lunch at Tsukiji Outer Market, the big MoD meeting in Ichigaya, then the send-off shabu-shabu at Suimei — where all six nationalities signed the menu and Doug got his farewell.

days.title: Tokyo to Kyoto: Fushimi Inari + Gion
days.summary: Shinkansen straight to Fushimi Inari, hiked deep into Mt. Inari — the vermilion torii corridor, the waterfall sub-shrines, the dragon whose head he patted like it was his dog Mercury — and helped two lost Singaporean strangers find their way down to the train. Then Kamogawa River dusk and yukata at the Kyoto hotel. Steinbeck's East of Eden rode along in his bag; its 'timshel,' the freedom to choose, rhymed with the whole trip.

days.title: Daiko-ji + Kyoto Trail + back to Tokyo
days.summary: A quiet culture wander before the climb: Marriott breakfast, then Daiko-ji, where Bryan found the Bussokuseki — the Buddha's Footprints stone — aligned his feet to the carved prints and prayed for his steps to be guided. Then Okazaki Park, the Nanzen-ji aqueduct path, and onto the Kyoto Round Trail at Higashiyama marker #37: root-covered forest, pink ribbon markers, and Max — a young Russian backpacker met on the trail, the prayer answered the way every mountain answered it, with someone to walk beside. Up to Himukai Daijingu, the 'Ise of Kyoto.' Down through Keage and a Cacao Market stop, then the Nozomi 28 back to Tokyo, 15:01 to 17:15 — the solo Kyoto trip was really Day 8 and this morning only. The Tokyo evening: a Pokemon Center haul of plushies and cards for the nieces and nephews, then a late dinner at a fifth-generation wagyu restaurant — the highest-rated one near the hotel, where a Middle Eastern family at the next table backed Bryan up on the halal beef.

days.title: Tsukiji morning + HND home
days.summary: The last morning: hotel packing, then a rainy walk through the Tsukiji Outer Market — Monzeki-dori, umbrellas, fishmongers, the famous tamago stalls. A 1877 Meiji-era plate on display in a tableware shop, a quiet sighting on the way out. Then the airport — lounge, gate, UA804 home. And the homecoming: the Japanese snack haul on the kitchen counter, the Pokemon plushies laid out on the couch, Kelly at the dining table going through every souvenir.
